speakerposition: topic
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of bill No. 166, to amend the Dominion Succession Duty Act.
Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, once more I register my protest against this kind of legislation. After the interprovincial conference in 1935 Mr. Dunning, who. was then minister of finance, came out with this same suggestion, which was also contained in the report of the Rowell-Sirois commission. I always felt that I was wrong when I supported Mr. Dunning, and! I could not accept the Sirois report, which was the apotheosis of soft brains. For these reasons I register my protest against legislation of this kind.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Bradette in the chair.
On section 1-Definitions.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: The trouble in regard to succession duties has been that when a person dies the executors make their filing, which goes down to the divisional office of the succession duties branch, and then after months and months and months- and months, as one hon. member beside me suggests-the department send out a notice that they are not satisfied with the return that has been made and they jump the assessment up by perhaps many thousands of dollars; not only that, but they charge interest on the amount from the time of death until the duty is paid. That is not right, because the executors do not know that the department will change the assessment or have different ideas about the amount of the estate. I feel that no interest should be charged on the unpaid balance until after a notice has been sent to the executors. The same thing applies to income tax on estates. I notice it in connection with the deferred tax for 1942. I got my notice the other day that my deferred tax for 1942 was so much, and due at time of death and. interest at eight per cent to be charged from date of death. I think that is very unjust.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: I think the hon. member has got two things mixed.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
No,
I am just saying that as regards succession duty and deferred income tax for 1942, the same rule applies. They go back to the time of death. I say that interest should be charged only from the time the notice has been sent out from the succession duty office.
100-338J

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: The minister should give some explanation as to why in the case of succession duties and income tax, interest is charged from a date anterior to the making of the assessment, rather than from the time of ascertaining what the liability is. This is an obnoxious feature of both laws -the charging of interest on an unascertained amount prior to assessment. I object to it. On principle it is bad. Under no statute I know of other than these two statutes, under no process of law that I know of, does interest begin to run, except by contract as in the case of a promissory note, or of special contract in the case of a special contract, until the liability at least is ascertained. That is a sound principle. This is a violation of that principle; it must be done simply for the purpose of screwing a little more money out of the taxpayers, and I object to it.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
I should-like to repeat the
protest I made when this matter was being discussed on the resolution, against the practice which is followed at the present time with respect to the use of the Dominion Succession Duty Act to force the filing of income tax returns. Have the officials of the department in charge of this particular act the right, once it is determined that an estate is not taxable, to refuse to issue the certificate until the personal representative has filed whatever income tax returns the income tax division feels justified in calling upon him to supply?

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
There is
no legal justification for that.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: I suggested before that if the matter of the income tax form and the administration of that department has to be tightened up it should be done under the provisions of the Income War Tax Act. I object most strenuously to this indirect method of forcing people to do something which they were not forced to do before this act was brought into effect. The question of dominion succession duties has nothing to do with income tax. I suggest that the administration is merely taking this indirect method of doing something which, if it is done, should be done in a direct way. Is the department within its legal rights in refusing to issue the certificate merely because the income tax division wants to have certain income tax forms filed by the personal representative?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
Of course the succession duty department is within its rights, as it only issues the certificate when the estate has been cleared up. The outstanding accounts of the estate are not definitely known until the income tax liability has been settled, and con-
Succession Duty Act

sequently the estate is not closed up until all outstanding accounts are provided for, and until the outstanding income tax liability is determined the estate cannot be finally settled. So that the succession duty branch has no other course than to make sure that all debts owing by the estate are accounted for before the estate is wound up.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: That is just-let me say-buncombe. There is no legal sanction for that in the statute, but they use their position, as being the same branch covering the two agencies, to force something which otherwise they could not force. Where is the legal sanction for the position the minister takes? There is none. I want an answer: is there any legal sanction for the position the minister is now taking? Point out the section of the statute which gives him the right. It is not there.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: If I may be allowed, we are dealing with bill No. 166, and I called section 1, which deals with "definitions".

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: I thought that was carried. There must be some place where succession duties can be discussed under this measure.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: It should have been done on the second reading of this bill.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: But on second reading you cannot cross-examine ministers. If the rule is going to be applied strictly, let us have it, but I think there should be enough leeway to air a grievance, and you cannot do it on second reading because, as I have said, you cannot crossexamine the minister.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: I believe the point has been stated here; the minister has answered; and I do not think we can allow this section to be used as one upon which the minister or myself can be cross-examined on all matters relating to succession duties. If that were the case, the moment you opened the act on one minor point you would have to traverse the whole subject-that at least is my belief- and I think that is going pretty far.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
If the
parliamentary assistant takes that attitude I do not think I can force his hand. But there is no legal sanction in our laws to-day for the attitude and the practice followed by the succession duty branch.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: There is no other section on which I can ask this question. I should like to know what rate of interest the succession duty branch charges on unpaid balance of duties.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: Five per cent.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: Then it is different from the 1942 deferred income tax rate, which is eight per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: No, the income tax rate is five per cent, and it was reduced to four per cent this year. This is a penalty section as well for income tax payments which are in arrears after the assessment has been made.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: On the 1942 notice it stated that it was eight per cent from time of death.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: That is after an assessment has been made, if payment is not made within a month an extra three per cent applies, bringing it to eight per cent.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: That is what I mentioned before. It says eight per cent from date of death.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: I am glad that the definition of "child" contained in subsection (b) has been widened, and I understand that the definition now corresponds to definitions of "child" "which appear in the succession duty acts of the several provinces. Because of that variation between the definitions in provincial succession duty acts and the Dominion Succession Duty Act, duty has been collected on estates where the beneficiaries were children within the meaning of the present definition. I mean that where a deceased had been in the position of loco parentis to a child but had not taken out papers, on his death that child is treated as a stranger and succession duty rates have been very much higher. I have in mind one case where the succession duty absorbed a very large portion of the cash which was in the estate and left the child, then eight years old, dependent upon certain property of doubtful value. What I should like to know is whether, in the interpretation of this clause, there is a possibility of its being regarded as retroactive so as to cover estates which have already been administered or returns filed since the inception of the act; or alternatively, is there any provision in the administration of the department for consideration of cases which have already been dealt with and for the granting of relief? I take it that that could well be done in view of the fact that parliament is now recognizing that the definition of "child" as contained in the original act was much too narrow.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
That question was considered, but it was decided that the proposed amendment would not be made retroactive. As things stand at the moment, therefore, it will apply only to estates which devolve from now on. It is pointed out that estates have

Succession Duty Act
been dealt with and the assets distributed on the basis of the law as it stood at that time, and for that among other reasons it was decided that this statute would not be given retroactive effect.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: It would not be of very wide application anyway.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: Not very wide, no, although I think it would have some considerable application. Representations were made that this extension should be given, that there were cases, as the hon. member for Regina City has pointed out, where the deceased stood in loco parentis but had never formally adopted the child he had been supporting for years, and it was felt that the benefit of the lower rates of exemptions under the succession duty act should be extended to that child.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: In any case where levies are made and have not been paid will they now be cancelled? I have in mind a very bad case, such as the hon. member for Regina City has mentioned, where land of dbubtful value was left to a beneficiary and actually a levy was made on that bequest under circumstances now covered by this act, which means that that beneficiary will ultimately have to pay for the land more than it is really worth. He has not yet paid, but the levy has stood1 against that land for the last five or six years. Will that levy be cancelled?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: I want to get the facts correctly. I understand that the estate devolved subsequent to the enactment of the act and that duties were assessed in accordance with the law as it now stands but have not yet been paid. My hon. friend wants to know whether those duties will be remitted if this amendment is carried. My answer would be that since the law is not being given retroactive effect, they could not be remitted. It would be putting that particular taxpayer [DOT] in a better position than one who paid his duty when it became due. I am giving that as my opinion now, rather as a legal opinion, and-1 do not know what the administrative action of the department will be. I doubt, however, whether .it would have legal authority to remit the amount of that tax which had accrued prior to the coming into force of the act.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
Generally speaking I am opposed to retroactive legislation, but I think the department might well consider that possibility having regard to this particular definition, in view of the fact that it is apparently the desire of the department to bring their definition of "child" into conformity with the definition of child as contained in the various provincial succession duty acts. For example,
we have in some provinces "child" treated the same as "natural child," where the rates of succession duty are very low, and under the dominion act treated as a stranger and the rates of duty are seven or eight times as great as they would be if the individual were assessed as a natural child.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: May I ask the parliamentary assistant whether he has checked up with regard to the facts I brought to the attention of the committee on the nineteenth? I pointed out that I had come across cases where dominion succession duty was levied against an interest bequeathed to a certain person by will and subsequently under the Testator's Family Maintenance Act of British Columbia other parties interested had been able to change that succession. The person to whom the bequest had been made, had his bequest cut down a great deal. There is no provision in the dominion act to cover such a case. The duty is levied just as though there had been no change under the provincial law. That is a very unfair situation and I think some provision should be put in the succession duty act to cover it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: I believe this question was raised the other day when we were in the resolution stage. The practice which is followed by the dominion succession duty authorities, and it seems probably the only practice which could be logically followed, is that they are governed by the provisions of the will or by the provisions of the statute in case of intestacy in the jurisdiction in which the estate devolves. The succession devolves as of the date of death and therefore the dominion considers that the liability to succession duty attaches on the assets of the estate as they existed at that time.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: Devolution under the law governs.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: Devolution under the law is what governs. If in certain jurisdictions there is statutory provision for varying the provisions of a will in order to provide maintenance for certain people it is felt that that is a matter of local convenience and the dominion succession duty law cannot properly take cognizance-

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: Can or cannot?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: -cannot take into account local arrangements.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
That is very unfair, because actually the devolution in the province is covered by the Testator's Family Maintenance Act in that case. In British Columbia we nave had an act of that type for perhaps fifteen years; the succession can be changed by
537S
Succession Duty Act

the Testator's Family Maintenance Act, provided that application is made, I believe, within six months after death.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
Where
there is a will.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: Yes. It gives power to vary the will. It enables the wife or the child to apply to have the will varied and is used in quite a few cases. I do not see what earthly right the dominion government has to refuse to recognize that provincial law. The provinces have the right to pass such laws and the dominion should' recognize them. There is just as much reason why the dominion should recognize the Testator's Family Maintenance Acts as that it should recognize the intestacy laws of a province. They are absolutely on the same footing, and I cannot understand why the dominion refuses to recognize these maintenance acts.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: Of course, I find it a little difficult to answer my hon. friend because in my own jurisdiction there is not a statute of that kind, but I understand it is really varying the devolution of the estate as provided by will or as provided by law. It is tantamount to a compromise between the beneficiaries which is confirmed by the court-

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: No; it is not a compromise at all.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: I appreciate that. But the various parties appear before the court and the court decides that the will did not provide for an equitable distribution, or that the law has not provided for it, and it can vary that distribution. It can also, I take it, in the terms of the order vary the apportionment of the death duties. Surely it would be competent for the court to do that. I am almost thinking aloud1, but it could make it a condition to the varying of the provision of the will that beneficiary A should receive fifty per cent of what wras provided in the will and that the person to whom the remaining fifty per cent of the legacy W'as transferred should pay a proportionately greater amount of any death duties that were levied, and if party A had been assessed for a greater amount he should be reimbursed that amount by party B to whom the transfer was made. It is indicated to me by the officials that they feel it is not practicable or desirable that any other basis should be taken for the assessment of dominion succession duties than the assets as they devolve on the date of death; and if there is a local statute which provides for varying that, then the local jurisdiction should make provision for the necessary adjustments of death duty liabilities or whatever other charges may attach to the estate.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: That is all right, but here is what happens. I know of one case in which the person actually paid the dominion succession duty on the bequest; in other words, the dominion government got the money, and then under the Testator's Family Maintenance Act the terms of the will were varied and the person who had already paid the succession duty has his bequest reduced. In some cases the reduction may be very large; it may even be wiped out by the order under the Testator's Family Maintenance Act of that province. Therefore you have the position of the dominion getting the money and the person not getting the bequest. That is obviously unfair. The provincial succession duty act provides for those orders that are made under the Testator's Family Maintenance Act, and there is no reason why the Dominion Succession Duty Act should not contain a similar provision. The provinces have the sole right to say how property will go. They can change the devolution as they see fit, and they have done it in some provinces. I think Ontario also has a Testator's Family Maintenance Act.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: That change in the law is made by the courts, of course.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: The change in the law is made by the provincial statutes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
The provincial statutes
authorize the courts to change the provision of the will, the devolution as provided by the will or as provided by the laws of intestacy.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: It is a method of distributing the estate just the same as the intestacy laws of the provinces which govern the manner in which an estate shall be distributed where there is no will. The Dominion Succession Duties Act should make provision for those orders made under the Testator's Family Maintenance Act.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
This involves a question of conflict of law. I think the parliamentary assistant has correctly stated the fundamental basis of the assessment. At the same time I am impressed by what the hon. member for Vancouver South has said, that it might work great injustice. I would suggest that the succession duty department work out some kind of arrangement with the authorities of British Columbia so as to avoid what would appear to be a manifest injustice. In my province we do not have any such laws as that. We do have a statute, which was passed by the legislature, relating to the devolution of intestate estates. I am not so sure that they were right, but they thought so and it is still the law. In the case of the death of an intestate leaving no issue but leaving a

Succession Duty Act
wife, she now gets a much larger share than she did under the old Devolution of Estates Act; and that might alter the incidence, because in that case I suggest the wife is in a preferred class, and the balance goes to, shall I say, the second or the third class, the collateral relatives. It alters the rate of taxation for succession duty purposes in the province.
I think this should be the subject of a conference with the provinces. In the meantime the law is as it is and it is not proposed to change it now.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: I think that is probably a good suggestion. My own view would be that the judges in those provinces which have legislation of the kind referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver South should bear in mind that the succession duty law-the dominion at any rate-provides that duties shall be assessed on the basis of the estate . as it devolves under the will or by the ordinary law, and that in making any orders such as have been indicated here the courts should impose an appropriate condition as to the adjustment of succession duty liability as between the various benefited parties.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: The statutes may not give them that right.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
I am in the dark on this.
May I ask the hon. member for Vancouver South what the provincial statute provides with respect to provincial succession duties in a case of that kind?

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
If I remember correctly, the provincial succession duty act recognizes an order made under the Testator's Family Maintenance Act and levies accordingly. The suggestion made by the parliamentary assistant would not work in all cases, because it might happen that the rate of succession duty would be changed. For example, if by order the money goes to a wife whereas it was bequeathed to a sister, the rate is changed.
It would not be fair to ask the judges- to take that into account. The Testator's Family Maintenance Act is a beneficial one. It protects the wife and children, and also the husband but no other relatives. These acts prevent a father from unfairly disinheriting his children or his wife and they have been very beneficial. I think the only way the difficulty can be remedied is to have a provision put in the Dominion Succession Duty Act. I know the government does not want to get money to which it is not entitled, yet that is what is happening under the present law.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: I have listened to my hon. friend. I am afraid I have been giving a lot of latitude here this morning. I protested before that we should keep within the section. This question whether a man is capable or incapable of making a will is a matter of property and civil rights which falls within the jurisdiction of the provinces. The dominion has no jurisdiction to say whether or not he is capable of making a will. Therefore it would be completely improper for the dominion government to be represented at any trial to determine whether a man was capable of making a will or not. I do not want to get into a long legal discussion here on testamentary capacity or anything else, but I do wish the committee would keep within the provisions of section 1, which extends and amplifies the definition of "child" as contained in the succession duty act.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 2-Gifts with reservation of benefit,

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
Subsection 1 of this section repeals the existing para-
53S0
Succession Duty Act

graph (d) of subsection 1 of section 3 of the act. It is in the nature of a benefit because there is an exemption from taxation through the limitation of three years. That applies where a gift is made and there is a bona fide possession and enjoyment and no reassumption by the donee. I think that is a proper provision. I am interested in the second subsection which adds a new subsection 4. This covers the case we were discussing on the resolution stage. It is quite clear now that it is the intention of the government to take authority to tax succession twice in a given set of circumstances.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: They are doing it now; this is really to confirm it.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: I doubt if they have the authority to do it. This is to make sure?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: That is correct.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: I doubt if they have authority to do that now. This is to make sure that where a person has a general power of disposition and does not exercise that power he shall be deemed to take succession in the first instance, and on his death the second succession occurs. That is exactly the situation in at least some of the provinces. Is that rule general in all the provinces, or only in some?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: I am told it is the rule in practically all.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: You do not know of any exception?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: No.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: It is just one of those cases where the thumbscrews are being turned a little in order to get more money for the crown. I should like to know if I understand the thing thoroughly. Of course, those who will have the liability in the first place will have to protect themselves with a proper instrument of disposition, that is, under their will. If a person in that situation makes a proper disposition and provides for alternative disposition in the event of the failure of the person to whom the power is given to appoint or dispose of the property, this situation will not arise.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: That is correct. If the power is general, then this section will operate, and section 31 as well.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: If there is a general power to appoint and he does appoint, will there still be double taxation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: Has that always been the law?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
I call my hon. friend's attention to section 31 of the act as it now stands, which reads:
Where a general power to_ appoint any property either by instrument inter vivos, or by will, or both, is given to any person, the duty levied in respect of the succession thereto shall be payable in the same manner and at the same time as if the property itself had been given, devised or bequeathed, to the person to whom such power is given.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: That means he pays on the devolution in the first instance?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: He is getting it just as though it was his own property.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: Not unless he takes a beneficial interest.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: He can do that under the general power.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: But if he does not get any benefit from it there are two sets of taxation. If he derives pecuniary benefits then I do not think there can be great Objection to his being taxed, but if he merely takes it in a fiduciary capacity and derives no personal benefit, there should not be double taxation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: The will should be drawn to prevent that.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: I agree that they will have to protect themselves by will.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: I am not clear about this; I was not able to hear all that was said. I should like to state a specific case and find out just what the answer will be. I mentioned this the last time we were discussing this matter. If a man by his will leaves his property to his wife for life with power of appointment and in the event that she fails to exercise that power, to a son or some children or somebody else, and the wife exercises that power, does she have to pay succession duty on the full estate and will the children or the persons to whom she leaves the property have to pay duty on the full estate on her death?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
I am assuming that the
power of appointment referred to is a limited power, that is, that the testator in his will gave the wife a life interest and provided that she might by her will appoint one or more of the children?

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
No. The testator by his will leaves it to his wife for life, and gives her a general power so that she may leave the property to whom she sees fit.

Succession Duty Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: Even to strangers?

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: To whom she sees fit.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
There would certainly be
two duties in that case. She would be assessed on her life interest and then on her death it would be treated as forming part of her estate.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
I think that matter should
be given further consideration because it is not fair. It amounts to double taxation. A man may have made that kind of will some time ago. He leaves his estate to his wife for life with a general power of appointment, and to his children if the wife fails to exercise that appointment. He lives for many years after his will is made, and dies, we will say, when he is seventy or seventy-two years of age. His wife is about the same age and survives him only for a year or two, having exercised her power of appointment. The result is that there would be two taxes on the whole estate within two or three years. The wife would have a life interest in the estate for two, three or four years and yet she would be taxed on the full estate. Then after that time her children, or whoever received the property, would be taxed again on the full estate. I think if the parliamentary assistant considers that matter he will come to the conclusion that it is not fair. I suggest that the section should not be passed in this form, that further consideration be given to the point. I protest against the section going through in its present form. Surely there should be some way of working this thing out so that it would be more equitable. The wife has had a life interest for only two or three years and she is taxed on the full value of the estate. Then there is a tax on the full value of the estate upon her death. That is not quite right. There should be some change made in this section to provide for a case of that kind.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
This is not really a change in the law. It is a qualifying provision in the definition section. Section 31 is quite clear with respect to the effect, from a succession duty point of view, of providing for a general power of appointment. Under section 31 that would appear to be clear. The case my hon.. friend has cited may appear, on the surface, to be a hard case. But the answer really is that a will should not be drawn in that way. It is all very well to say that the widow is given a life interest. But in fact she is given complete and1 free distribution of the corpus of the estate, because there is no restriction on her right of disposition. The testator has indicated, it is true, to whom he would like the property to go if she does not see fit to exercise her power of disposition.
But she is perfectly free to leave it to a complete stranger. I should not think my hon. friend would suggest that under those circumstances there should not be a tax imposed, if she did exercise that power of appointment. What he is suggesting is that if she fails to exercise it there should not be a tax. The point is as to whether the testator has absolute freedom in exercising the power of appointment. That is the test. It seems to me it is a reasonable test; and if the legal profession or testators are aware of the law they will be governed accordingly in drawing wills.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
I do not suggest that the widow should escape taxation. But I submit she should be taxed only on the life interest.
I think that is the stand that the parliamentary assistant took, and that is what he had in mind the other day when this matter was discussed. This is what was said on that occasion:
Mr. Hazen: That is what I want to understand clearly. Does she pay on her life interest or does she have to pay on the full value of the estate?
Mr. Abbott: She pays on her life interest in the estate, and in Quebec-I do not know about the dominion-it is based on her life expectancy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: That is correct.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: That is what it should be. It should be a life interest, based on the life expectancy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
That is what would happen.
A testator may provide this: "I leave my wife a life interest in the residue of my estate, and on her death to go to my children in such proportion as she may determine"-or even just "to my children". In that case the . widow would be taxed only on her life interest, based on her life expectancy; and the duty would1 be assessed on the children who received the ownership of the residue on the death of their mother, in accordance with the rules applicable generally. That is exactly what would happen if a testator did not give to his wife a general power of appointment. In effect, it is almost surplusage to say it is giving her life interest, and it is giving her complete freedom to dispose of the property.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: Well, as a matter of fact, is it? I do not think it is the same as giving her the estate outright, by any means. She cannot do as she likes with it. In a sense she is a trustee; she cannot go and spend the money. She only has the use of the income to that extent for her life.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
What is to prevent her using the proceeds herself? She has general
53S2
Succession Duty Act

power of appointment, and she can do what she sees fit. Who cam attack her, or who can attack her estate?

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: There is something in that, but-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: It is a form of giving her free disposition.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: But why should there be a difference between a man who leaves a will saying, "I leave my estate to my wife, and then to my children", and the man who uses this other form, saying, "I leave my estate to my wife for life with power of appointment, and then, failing that, to my children." In the one case if the will says, "to my wife and then to my children" she pays only on the life interest. Then the children have to pay on the corpus of the estate. But in the other case she has to pay on the whole estate, and then the children have to pay on the whole estate. Then she may die only two or three years after the husband. I think that to some extent we are playing with words. If the first proposition is fair, that she should be taxed only on her life expectancy, then this is clearly wrong. I do not think they should go through this procedure.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: The real effect of the section is to prohibit, for succession duty purposes, a general power of appointment without restriction. The succession duty act says in effect: If you wish to make that kind of power, so far as taxation is concerned it is as though you had not appointed at all. That is the effect of the law at the present time. This amendment is simply to clarify what might be considered as a conflict between two sections. The law now provides that if a man makes a general power of appointment to a beneficiary, that is considered as constituting a disposition of the property, wdien the power is exercised.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: There should be a qualifying section to protect widows in cases such as I have mentioned. As it stands, I can only say it is not fair or right. The parliamentary assistant says that a will should be drawn in a different way, to get around the difficulty. Well, many people have had their wills drawn for years. They do not know about this provision. When they die their widows will have to pay the full value of the estate, and a year or two later perhaps the children have to pay the full value.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: I am advised that that is the law in all the provinces of Canada.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
That does not make it one bit better. It has been held by the courts

that it is perfectly within the competence of any testator to protect himself against any injustices which it may be considered would flow from the provision respecting a general power of appointment, when permitted for purposes of succession duty.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
I wish to say a word cn this matter. I note that this paragraph-I believe it is paragraph (d)

has been amended to provide that-
Property taken under a gift whenever made of which actual and bona fide possession and enjoyment has not been assumed by the donee or by a trustee for the donee at least three years before the death of 'the deceased.
I have no quarrel with that position. But what I would like to know is this: Is there any exemption with respect to what might be called normal expenditures, or gifts normal in relation to the status of income of the man making the gifts? I have in mind, for example, the matter of a small disbursement, possibly the giving of $100 or $50. Suppose I give my child $10 to-day, and I die within another year; would that have to be revealed in my succession duty return and succession duty paid on it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
There is a provision in the act which governs the case to which my hon. friend has referred. I will direct his attention to section 7, which says:
7. (1) From the dutiable value of any property included in a succession the following exemptions shall be deducted and no duty Bihall be leviable in respect thereof.
And paragraph (f) states:
In respect of a gift made by the deceased where the same is proved 'to have been absolute and to have taken effect in the lifetime of the deceased, to have been part of his ordinary and normal expenditure, and to have been -reasonable having regard to the amount of his income and the circumstances under which the gift was made.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Bill reported.
Mr. ABBOTT moved the third reading of the bill.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to go back to the point I raised when this bill was in committee and1 I was ruled out of order. I pointed out at the resolution stage that the dominion succession duty office has to issue a certificate before the assets of an estate can be released to the person who represents it. Take the simple example of a life insurance policy. If a testator leaves to his widow a life insurance policy of say three thousand dollars, obviously it is not taxable for succession duty, but before the

Succession Duty Act
53S3
necessary certificate is issued by the dominion succession duty office to permit the life insurance company to pay the money to the widow or the personal representative of the estate or to some beneficiary who is named direct, the department has to give to the personal representative of the estate a release, which he turns over to the insurance company and then obtains the money. Practically in every instance where the testator has not filed income tax returns during say the last three or four years prior to his death, the department says to the personal representative of the estate: You cannot have that money and that release until you satisfy us that the testator during those years had no taxable income. It may be that every proper method should be used to ensure that testators have complied with all the provisions of the income tax law, but the thing to which I object is that the government is using an indirect method of obtaining the filing of income tax returns. If income tax returns are not being filed as provided for under the law, the dominion government should bring in amendments to the income tax act. I submit that it is absolutely illegal to hold up the granting of the certificate, once it is determined that the estate is not taxable for succession duty, until the personal representative has complied with the provisions of the income tax act. If there is any provision in the Dominion Succession Duty Act or in any other act of this parliament which allows the succession duty office to follow this procedure I should be glad to be informed about it. In my view the administration should not do indirectly something that they can do directly.
I know that the parliamentary assistant said a short while ago when the bill was in committee : The estate has not been wound up yet and until all the debts have been satisfied, including income tax, the department could not issue the certificate. Before the Dominion Succession Duty Act was made the law of this country there was no similar means available to the administration for collecting income tax and there is no reason why now, just because this machinery has been set up, it should be used for the purpose of obtaining something that is owing to another department.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: Is my hon. friend speaking particularly of an estate where it is clear that no tax is payable, or including estates where the tax is payable?

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: No, I was using that as an illustration to show how the succession duty act machinery was being used.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: His argument would have more force if he was speaking particularly of an estate where no tax was payable.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
I was taking as an illustration the small estates such as I run into in the province from which I come. In that pro'vince there are many thousands of people who have never had enough income in the last ten years to warrant the filing of income tax returns. The income tax branch knows that there are thousands of farmers in Saskatchewan who have not filed income tax returns because they have not sufficient income to be liable to the tax. I am not saying that the returns should not be filed. The fact remains that the widows know nothing about their late husband's affairs. They may have a little bit of insurance coming to them, and that is held up until the widow digs around and tries to obtain a lot of information with respect to her husband's farming operations in the last few years. Payment of the insurance is held up for some considerable time, and in some cases the widow needs that money badly. I suggest that the succession duty branch has not jurisdiction to hold up the granting of the release merely because the income tax branch insists on the filing of certain returns.
The parliamentary assistant a short time ago referred to cleaning up an estate. If his argument holds good, the whole estate should be held up until all the creditors have been taken care of.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: Until the amounts owing to the creditors are known.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: That is immediately known, because a list of the debts is usually filed at the time the succession duty papers are filed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: An additional debt may be the income tax liability.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: That would only reduce the amount of the estate. It certainly would not otherwise affect the succession duty payable. I submit that if it is obvious that the estate is below the amount that is taxable for succession duty, no matter how much may be owing for income tax, the certificate should be granted.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext: The hon. member's argument would have more force with respect to an estate not liable to succession duties than with regard to estates where duties are payable.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
I do not want to prolong the discussion. I merely want to register my protest against using this machinery to do something indirectly which, if the administration believes it should be done, can be done
Succession Duty Act

directly by an amendment to the income tax act. I do not believe that this machinery should be used in the manner I have indicated.

maintopic: DOMINION SUCCESSION DUTY ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the department should be congratulated on their efforts to collect the income tax. The hon. member has referred to a case where the estate consisted of 83,000, but you could easily bring into the discussion a ease where the estate was 850,000. If that man had never paid any income tax and the succession duty branch issued the release, the proceeds of the estate would be distributed without seeing that any income tax was paid, and there would be many oases where they would find later on that the testator should have paid income tax. In the meantime the money has been distributed and there would be no one to collect the income tax from. If there is nothing in the statutes at the present time to deal with cases of that kind. I feel that the department are justified in using this method, but I do suggest that if there is nothing in the statutes already to take care of that situation an amendment should be made to the act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution: That it is expedient to amend the Civil Service Superannuation Act and to provide for the extension of the operation of the said act to certain persons in the public service not 
presently included therein and to make such further provisions respecting contributions, allowances and benefits as may be deemed necessary for the said purpose and for the better operation or administration of the said act.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: CIVIL SERVICE SUPERANNUATION
subtopic: EXTENSION OF OPERATION OF ACT-FURTHER PROVISIONS AS TO CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
(Winnipeg North Centre): My reason for speaking on this measure at the resolution stage arises out of my concern that the bill should cover certain classes of employees in the public service. I have not yet, of course, seen the bill, and I do not know how far it goes. In many instances we find it desirable to agree to a resolution without much discussion and to delay comment until the bill comes down, but in this instance I feel it is desirable .to make a few comments now, in the hope that if the people I am concerned about are not included in the bill the government will have the opportunity to include them before the bill is introduced. In other words, it is quite satisfactory to me if when the bill comes down these people are covered and the government is in a position to take the credit unto itself. I am not worried about that, but I am concerned about certain classes of employees in the public service.
The first group about which I wish to speak is those who are employed at the printing bureau, especially those of the printing and mechanical trades. Up to the present time they have not been included in the terms of the Civil Service Superannuation Act. Nevertheless amongst the employees at the printing bureau are a considerable number who have been there a very long time. I have figures as to the length of service of the employees of the printing bureau as at December 1, 1942; and I find that at that time there were in the printing and mechanical departments of the bureau 384 employee^. Of these, 60 had a service of five years or under, 128 had service between five and twenty years, 131 had service between twenty and thirty years, and 65 had service between thirty and fifty years. Yet despite those long records of service these employees, because they are paid on a weekly rate rather than at an annual rate, have been excluded from the benefits of the Civil Service Superannuation Act.
On August 21 of last year these employees presented a brief to the Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty), the minister charged with the administration of the department in which they are employed, wherein they set out their case and asked for an interview with the Secretary of State. There are some portions of their brief which I feel should be drawn to the attention of the administration. They

Civil Service Superannuation
indicated that these employees fall into two groups as far as these representations are concerned:
(a)	Employees of the printing trades. These employees hold positions on the regular establishment of the department as authorized by the civil service commission and who have been appointed thereto under the provisions of the Civil Service Act, and ivhose rates of pay are determined under section 16 of chapter 152, R.S.C. 1927 (Public Printing and Stationery Act), and afterwards confirmed by order in council;
(b)	Employees of the mechanical trades. These employees occupy positions which are exempt from the provisions of the Civil Service Act. The positions are authorized by treasury board following a recommendation of the civil service commission. Appointments thereto are made by the minister, and the continuation of positions and employment are authorized by the treasury board from year to year.
The employees at that point went on in their brief to set out their reasonable desire to provide themselves with a measure of security against the hazards of death and premature displacement, in a manner similar to that provided to other employees in the public service. They dealt with some of the technical difficulties which they had been told stood in the way, and urged as strongly as they could that consideration be given to their case. They concluded their brief with a request for an interview with the Secretary of State. Their brief was signed on behalf of the employees by G. Y. Armstrong, president, and J. T. Clancey, secretary; the name of the organization is the Department of Public Printing and Stationery Welfare Association.
A short time after that, on September 8, 1943, a committee of that association was granted an interview with the Secretary of State to discuss this brief to which I have referred. Following that interview the matter was referred to the treasury board by the Secretary of State for its consideration. Later on the association was asked to have representatives appear before Mr. W. C. Ronson for an interview, and on November 2, 1943, and as a result of this meeting with Mr. Ronson, a memorandum was submitted to Mr. Edmond Cloutier, the King's Printer. I should like to give the text of this memorandum. It is dated November 15, 1943, and is addressed to the King's Printer:
Dear Sir:
re Superannuation
In connection with the above subject concerning the employees in the printing and mechanical trades of the government printing bureau, and as a result or the suggestion by Mr. W. C. Ronson, assistant deputy minister of finance, at our joint conference on Tuesday, November 2, 1943, we are submitting the following for your consideration.
1.	That a separate scheme of superannuation be established for this class of employee to include employees of both the printing and mechanical trades who are in positions of continuing indeterminate duration and on the basic staff.
2.	That all conditions with respect to wages, overtime and hours of work to remain as at present.
3.	That for the purposes of contributions an annual salary be established on the basis of the weekly basic rate multiplied by 52.
The employees feel this to be one of the important hurdles to be got over, and their proposal is a quite simple one, namely, that their weekly rate be treated as an annual rate by the simple process of multiplying it by 52.
4.	That employees of three years' service who, though not on the basic staff, are considered to be in positions of a continuing indeterminate duration, be considered eligible for superannuation.
5.	That the age for retirement be set at 60 for males and 55 for females with the privilege of extensions to the age of 65 years according to the provisions of section 10 of the Civil Service Superannuation Act.
6.	That contributions, benefits and other terms of retirement to be similar to those of the present Civil Service Superannuation Act (chapter 24, R.S.C., 1927).
Trusting this will receive your favourable consideration,
Respectfully yours,
G. V. Armstrong, President. J. T. Clancey, Secretary.
The printing and mechanical employees of the bureau do not know yet just how matters stand. I have a particular interest in their case because I happen to be a member of the trade union of which a great many of the employees in the printing bureau are also members. Their hope is that as a result of their interview with the Secretary of State, as a result of their interview with Mr. Ronson, and as a result of the further representations they have made in this matter, the bill which is to be introduced on the basis of this resolution will meet their views.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that no technicality should stand in the way of men and women, with the length of service that these employees have, being treated similarly to other employees in the public service. We in this House of Commons ought to be interested in these people. They play a very important part in the life of parliament. Sometimes, as a popular indoor sport, we blame the printer for things that appear which a member thinks are not exactly as he said them. But speaking as a printer, I say, "We can take it." As a matter of fact, considering the pressure under which the bureau has to work, considering the short space of time in which we expect Hansard and other printed material
53S6
Civil Service Superannuation

to appear, I feel that the employees over there do a very good job. I say that despite the fact that once in a while I have been the victim of a typographical error. That is really nothing to worry about, and I want to pay this tribute to the work of my printing colleagues.
While paying that tribute I might take a moment to pay another tribute and that is to our friends the Hansard reporters. It is sometimes another popular indoor sport to blame them for getting down incorrectly some of the things hon. members say. But there too I feel, especially in the light of the cross-fire we have sometimes in this house, that they do an awfully good job in getting it down as well as they do, and I hope that if on occasion we make corrections in what they take down they will know that really we appreciate the high quality of their work.
Now I think I will leave the case of the printers at that. I hope it will be covered in the bill when it comes down. If these employees are not included in the bill as it is now drafted, I hope the government will delay it a day or two to make sure that, a piece of injustice that has been perpetrated on these employees will be corrected at this time.
Just one other sentence about the case of the printing employees. I will quote section 6 of their brief of August 21, 1943:
6. We are quite willing to accept the terms of the act, including the obligation to contribute six per centum of our -wages to the fund.
There- are certain other groups that should be included in this bill as well. Perhaps they are already there. If so, that is fine; but if they are not there, one has to speak now in order to have one's representations considered. This time I appeal on behalf of a large number of railway mail clerks. I understand that several hundreds-I believe as a matter of fact they run to four thousand across t'he country-of the railway mail clerks are still under the retirement act of 1896, and their desire is to* be transferred to the superannuation act of 1924. I am told that these employees some years ago were given the opportunity to transfer to this other act but. rejected it, and it is has been said to them that, having rejected it, it is their own fault and they should not now complain. But they point out that after they rejected the offer to transfer to the superannuation act of 1924 certain things were done in connection with the funds under the retirement act of 1896, and the most striking thing that was done, I am told, was the reduction of the interest rate from five per cent to four per cent, which was effected about 1932 or 1933. That

change has had the effect of reducing the value of the pensions that these employees can draw under that fund, and they tell me that they have not had an opportunity to transfer to the other fund since that very striking change was made in 1932 or 1933. These employees have made strong but very reasonable representations, and I imagine from the wording of one communication I received some time ago that all the Manitoba members of this house received the document I have. They have also made their appeal to the government. On their behalf I -wrote on two occasions to the Minister of Finance and on the second occasion I received a fairly hopeful letter dated April 26 of this year:
Dear Mr. Knowles:
I wish to acknowledge your letter of April 21 with further reference to .the question of superannuation for the Winnipeg railway mail clerks association.
You will remember that the Prime Minister announced in the house a day or two ago that the Civil Service Superannuation Act would form part of the legislation still to be brought before the House of Commons. When this act is being reviewed, your representations will be given careful consideration.
Yours very truly,
J. L. Ilsley.
I earnestly hope that my representations were given consideration. I hope that the bill in the form in which it has been drafted includes the granting of this request. If so,, that is fine and my speech at this moment is unnecessary; but if it is not in the bill, my reason for speaking now is to urge the government to give further consideration to this request with a view to meeting it when the bill based upon this resolution is brought down.
Not only- are there the classes of public servants to which I have already referred, but in a good many departments of government we have people who have been working for many years and yet technically are so identified that they do not come under the Civil Service Superannuation Act. For example, I hold in my hand a brief written on behalf of employees of the Deer Lodge hospital, which comes under the administration of the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. . Mackenzie). There are some other matters in this brief that I shall bring to his attention when his estimates are before the house, but at this moment I refer only to this fact. This brief refers to other employees as well, but in particular to the so-called temporary permanents. Employees of that class, no matter how many years they may be working for the government, are denied entry into the Civil Service Superannuation Act. It seems to me it

Civil Service Superannuation
53S7
is possible under the terms of the resolution we are discussing for the government to put provisions in the bill to take care of some of these people.
Another group of people who feel that they are dealt with unfairly, under present conditions, if I understand them correctly, are the employees who transfer from one classification to another. They find that although both positions are classified as permanent in the Civil Service Act, they are required to resign from their first position and are subsequently reappointed as temporary employees in the new positions. When that happens, the employee who formerly was permanent and had certain benefits, such as pension rights, finds that he loses all the benefits of permanency that he previously enjoyed, even though he may have had many years of continuous satisfactory service. In other words, an employee frequently must choose between remaining in a position of a lower grade at a lower salary with pension rights or taking the better position which he is capable of filling, but in doing so losing all of his rights of permanency, including his pension benefits. I hope that there are provisions in the bill which will meet that situation. As I have said several times already, if they are not there I plead with the government to redraft the bill before it is introduced in the house.
When the estimates of the Department of Public Works were before the committee the other day I had occasion to make representations on behalf of women doing char work in public buildings. I now wish to say a word on behalf of the men doing char work in this building. Many of them have been here for many- years, but for some technical reason they are not treated as permanent employees; at least they are not included in the provisions of the Civil Service Superannuation Act. Some of those men have been here five, eight, nine years, some longer. Some of them, who have been here longer than nine years had the interesting experience of being dismissed in 1935 after the election and then being rehired after a fuss was made over their dismissal. But they are still temporary employees. Amongst other benefits that are denied them, they do not come within the terms of any superannuation or pension fund provided by the government. There are other employees of the government in this building who are in the same box, the messenger staff and others employed in the service of the House of Commons.
We are hearing much these days that sounds very good to our ears about the rights of persons over property; about the new concept of social security. We listened' to am interesting and fighting speech by the Prime Minister yesterday about the new order which he desires to help fashion. I suggest that one place to start fashioning the new order with its concept of social security is right on our own doorstep. I suggest that we should not have a number of groups of people working for the government itself who are discriminated against, as is the case with some of those people I have mentioned1. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I hope that when this bill comes down it will look as though this speech of mine did not need to be made. But I express in the meantime a wish that if any of the groups I have referred to are not covered in the terms of the bill, or indeed if there are other government employees whose situations are similar, the government will redraft the bill and really put into effect some of the ideas that it is now proclaiming about the new order, about social security, about the responsibility of employers to their employees, and about the rights of people to enjoy freedom from want and freedom from fear.

maintopic: CIVIL SERVICE SUPERANNUATION

I wish to associate myself with what has been said by the previous speaker (Mr. Knowles). I hope that when the bill is introduced it will contain some provision to take care of large groups of civil servants who were favourably reported on two years ago by a special committee. I refer to those who have been paying into retirement funds over a long period of years. In certain instances some individuals have been picked out and consideration has been given to them.
The previous speaker has fully covered -the situation. We could go on and elaborate on other groups, but I wish to mention particularly that group who for a long period of years, because of misunderstanding, failed to elect to be included under superannuation benefits. Some yeans ago they sought to have a last opportunity to elect. I do feel that that class should be given another opportunity to elect. I hope that the bill will include those groups so that the matter can be fairly and finally settled and we shall n'ot have a recurrence of this discussion from time to time.
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): I should like to say a word so there will be no misunderstanding about this measure. I can assure hon. members that the representations to which they have seen fit to give publicity in this house to-day have long been before the government for consideration. There would hardly be any occasion for bringing in a bill at all if it were not to deal with the representations that had been made.
53S8
Civil Service Superannuation

The general purposes of this bill are, first of all, to allow any person who previously at any time was given the right to come under the superannuation act during a certain period to have another period of one year from October 1 to exercise his option. That will apply to some thirty-five hundred persons who are still members of the retirement fund, which really was not a pension scheme but a compulsory savings scheme, whereby the members thereof got back with interest the amount of the deductions from their pay during their period of service. There are, as I say, still about thirty-five hundred persons who for some reason or other did not choose to come under the superannuation act at the time it was passed1, though they were given the opportunity for first of all a period of two years, and then one additional year, to exercise the option to do so. A further period of one year from October 1, 1944 is to be allowed them to exercise the option now. The bill will also provide for the cases of contributors who had service prior to the time they became contributors and would have had the option of taking credit for such period of service. Each had a period of three months during which upon becoming a contributor he could elect to bring in the period of service he had before that time. Of course, he would have to make the proper contribution. He is to be given a further period of one year from October 1, 1944, to elect as to whether or not he wants to have the benefit of the period prior to the time he became a contributor.
The third major provision is to take care of those who could not become contributors to the superannuation fund because they were not permanent employees with a stated annual salary, those who are generally called prevailing rates employees. There is a fourth group of sections which provide for certain increases in the benefits. First of all, there is the right to the return of the aggregate contributions without interest on retirement at any time. Formerly one had to be ten years in the service to be entitled to a return of the contributions made if he left the service.
When a pension becomes payable to dependents under the terms of the act and runs out before the aggregate of the total contributions have been paid as a pension, the pension will be continued until it has equalled the contributions made by the former public servant. If there are no dependents of a public servant a minimum return will be made to his estate of an amount equal to the contribution he has made to the fund.
Provision is being made for the dropping of what was called the forfeiture clause for

dismissal for misconduct or, what was regarded as misconduct, for political partisanship. Other punitive action may have to be taken in regard to the misconduct of a public servant, but it will be in some other form than the confiscation of his contributions to the pension fund.
A large number of recommendations were made by the special committee which sat in 1939. Immediately following the report of that special committee an order in council was passed implementing certain of the recommendations. Chapter 27 of the statutes of 1940 gave statutory effect to the order in council. The present bill consists of a consolidation of the provisions of that order in council, which was not very clearly drawn in the first instance. The other part of the bill will implement the main recommendations of the committee of 1939. I feel confident that when the bill-which is a lengthy one, and may appear rather complicated because it deals with many amendments to the existing act necessary for concordance-is before hon. members they will find that careful and sympathetic consideration has been given to the representations made, not only by the group referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre but by the various organizations of civil servants who on more than one occasion conferred with the special committee of the cabinet in respect to their grievances.
