speechtext:
I understand the minister has received a brief from the British Columbia industrial and' scientific research council in
Supply-Trade and Commerce

which they ask for a grant to aid in their work. In their brief they point out that in the course of an address to the Canadian chemical conference on June 7, 1944, the president of the national research council made this statement:	__
We must have in Canada sufficient laboratory facilities to deal with every demand, and that is not now the case. [DOT] The present council is not in favour of a policy of centralization of all such facilities. It is felt that laboratories to serve particular regional needs should be located in the regions concerned.
Apparently provision has been made for the establishment of what is known as the prairie regional committee of the national research council. A sum to help that organization is included in this year's estimates. This brief requests that similar assistance be given to the British Columbia industrial and scientific research council. On this council are representatives of the dominion government. There is one representative from the federal Department of Mines and Resources, one from the Department of Fisheries and one from the national research council. What is the attitude of the government toward this request for assistance in connection with the work of the British Columbia industrial and scientific research council?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have not before me the letter or the memorandum attached to the letter received from the Hon. Mr. Carson, the Minister of Trade and Industry of British Columbia. However, I dealt with the matter this morning by saying all I could say at the moment, namely that I had called a meeting of the privy council committee on industrial and scientific research. That meeting will be held next Tuesday, and the matter will be considered.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Is it a fact that the policy of the national research council is against centralization and rather in favour of building up research facilities in different parts of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: I do not think that I would say the policy of the national research council is opposed to centralization. I can say however that it is in favour of broadening the present arrangement. The next item in the estimates is proof of that suggestion, because in that item we ask for funds to establish a branch of research work in one of the three western provinces. I believe it would be correct to say it is important that the national research council keep in close touch with any research work in Canada, wherever it may be done, so as to avoid duplication.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
The minister has referred to the next item, the purpose of which, I suggest, is not obvious. May I at this point, however, make some brief observations in connection with item 357, and what I shall now say might be taken as covering both items. It is dear to most hon. members that the vote now before the committee is one of the most important. I believe all can agree that the work done by scientific research in the last number of years has been of inestimable value to Canada.
When we think of the millions of dollars that have been saved by our scientists in the . improvement of our crops, for example, through the eradication of many diseases which used to afflict them, it will be agreed that this amount of money and even a great deal more could very well be spent to improve the general welfare of the people of Canada. I suggest, following the lead given by the minister a few minutes ago, that in view of the peculiar conditions existing in western Canada and the great amount of work which has to be done in the prairie provinces in connection with the crops, the recommendations which have been made to the administration should be immediately accepted and an extensive laboratory set up in the prairie provinces. I suggest that the best location would be in the city of Saskatoon, from which I come. It is in the very centre of the prairie provinces, it is a university city, and one from which a great many of our leading scientists have come.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: And a good member of parliament.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
When the government was seeking to replace General McNaughton as head of the research council it was to the city of Saskatoon and the Saskatoon university they went to pick an able administrator and eminent scientist in the person of Mr. C. J. Mackenzie. That indicates the calibre of the men that we have in that part of the country, and men who are well versed in the types of problems with which we are confronted in the prairie provinces. I suggest, therefore, that the government consider setting up an extensive type of laboratory in that part of the country to deal with the problems which face the people of the prairie provinces, who in the last few years have become more and more conscious of the fact that if we are ever to develop a diversified economy it can be done only through the utilization of the various kinds of crops that are produced in the prairie provinces along lines which probably we have not heretofore

Supply-Trade and Commerce
followed. I therefore strongly recommend the establishment of such a laboratory in Saskatoon.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
I hope the minister will say something in reply to the comments which I made, I believe yesterday, when this item was before the committee. I pointed out at that time that I felt that not sufficient funds had been provided to make it possible for the scientists of the national research council to do all the research and other work which they should be doing, and of which they are eminently capable. I want to take a moment to pay as high a tribute as one possibly can to what some of our scientists have done at that institution, particularly during the course of the war. The minister knows, as do other hon. members, that a number of inventions which have aided materially in the conduct of the war, and particularly in the saving of life, have grown out of research at this institution.
Another matter which has been brought to my attention about the research council is that there has been considerable uncertainty as to the status of the men there with respect to military call-ups. I can appreciate the difficulty in this connection. I think all of us must appreciate the embarrassing position in which the men find themselves, for even when higher-placed officials make it known to them that they are doing an important job and should stay with it, there is the pressure ' of their own feelings in the matter and their desire to be with their colleagues and college classmates in the front line, which results in many of these men leaving their posts with the council to go on what is known as active service. I suggest that some more definite effort should be made to convince these men that they are on active service in the work they are doing at the research council and should be encouraged to carry on with it.
During the debate on the budget resolutions something was said about the importance of encouraging research work throughout Canada by private corporations. I believe the government should be doing all it can on its own initiative to encourage research work. This is a matter upon which I should like to hear from the minister. I hope he will have some announcement to make as to plans for enlarging the w'ork of the council and for providing better salaries so that we may attract into this work many of the brilliant young men who are coming out of our universities.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre speaks of the difficulties, of which he apparently has some knowledge, with respect to enlistments from the staff of the national research council. He speaks about some persuasion being used to show them that their duty lies in civilian activities. May I observe that this condition can hardly be laid at the doorstep of the minister who is now attempting to get his estimates through; rather it is a product of the man-power plan which this country has been following, as I believe mistakenly, through these years.
Will the minister state whether there is a permanent head of the national research council, or whether the position is now temporary?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
Dealing first with the remarks of the leader of the opposition, the president of the national research council is General McNaughton. As we all know he is not acting at the present time; the acting president is Dean Mackenzie.
I have given some consideration to the remarks made yesterday by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre; and I would state, briefly, that the national research council has always recognized the need for maintaining a proper balance between fundamental research, or pure research as it is sometimes called, and applied research.
On many occasions attention has been called to the importance of maintaining this balance by members of the national research council, when questions of policy and programmes were under consideration. It has been emphasized that practical, or applied research, is based upon and dependent upon the fundamental knowledge acquired through pure research, and that a national research programme must provide for both fundamental and applied1 research in proper balance.
In the past some fundamental research has been carried on by the national research council in its own laboratories; but a still larger volume of such work has been sponsored and stimulated by the council through grants in aid of research, awarded to members of staffs of Canadian universities, qualified to conduct scientific research and1 having laboratory facilities at their disposal. Such grants are not restricted to fundamental research projects, but most of the work carried on under them has been of that type. Such grants not only stimulate the acquiring of fundamental knowl-

edge, but assist in the post-graduate training of young scientists in research methods, and also assist in the development of post-graduate instructions in scientific research.
During the abnormal conditions imposed by war, with need for the solution of practical problems confronting the armed services and other war establishments, it has been necessary for the national research council to direct most of its activities to applied research, but it is the definite policy of the council, as soon as

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, July 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie King for the second reading of bill No. 161, to provide for family allowances.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
maintopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENTS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN UNDER SIXTEEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no need to stress the importance of the family allowance bill to members of this house or to the people of Canada. This bill has been put forward by the government as part of the comprehensive scheme of social legislation forecast in the speech from the throne. The bill has already been supported not only by members of the government and by members of this house who support the government, but it has

Family Allowances
also been generously supported 'by the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party in the house (Mr. Coldwell) and also by the member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion). Their reservations on points of detail can be dealt with better in committee, but perhaps'I may have a word or two later to say about some of them in the course of my remarks.
Only the Progressive Conservative party has so far opposed this measure in this house or throughout the country, and I venture to say that like the Conservative press, some of which has been critical of the measure in some respects or in totality, the opposition of the Progressive Conservative party as voiced yesterday by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) and by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) is based not only on failure to understand the measure but as well on the failure to realize its importance as the greatest single means to meet a fundamental need of our people in these changed and changing times. The speeches of the leader of the opposition and of the hon. member for Parkdale are important, but important only for the reason that they show to all the people of Canada how fundamental is the difference in outlook towards the social and the humanitarian questions with which the people of Canada are concerned as between those hon. gentlemen and the Liberal party and this government.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENTS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN UNDER SIXTEEN
speechtext: You have no monopoly on that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
maintopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENTS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN UNDER SIXTEEN
speechtext:
We have no monopoly on anything. When the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Parkdale voice views such as they voiced yesterday, I am entitled to say that they mark a fundamental cleavage between themselves and this party, and that cleavage will be recognized more and more by the people of Canada as the days go by.
But I believe that the house and the people of Canada are far less interested in the views of members of the opposition, as voiced yesterday, than they are in the merits of this proposal, and they want to consider this measure on its merits. They want to see what it is, they want to see what it will do, and they want to see how it will work; and I shall try in my remarks this afternoon to deal in some measure with these three questions.
It is generally recognized, not only in this country but in other countries as well, that Canada has led the world in the economic and financial conduct of its war effort and in the equitable distribution of the costs of the war. With family allowances as proposed in this bill, Canada again leads the world. Canada
leads the world in making adequate provision for her greatest single asset, the three and a half million children of our country.
The proposal itself is that a parent maintaining a child resident in Canada, within the definition of the act, shall each month receive, whether in Nova Scotia or British Columbia, or in any other part of Canada, $5 for each child less than six years of age; $6 for each child between the ages of 6 and 9; $7 for children of 10 to 12; and $8 for children from 13 to 15; less $1 for the fifth child, $2 for the sixth and seventh, and $3 for each additional child. At this moment I wish to correct an impression which the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay left, that in the consideration of the number of children for the purpose of reduction according to the act we would consider children oyer the age of sixteen. If the hon. member will look at the definition of "child" in section 2 (a) of the bill he will find that a child is defined as a person less than sixteen years of age, so that adequately clears up any misunderstanding he may have on that point.
I	ask hon. members, all of whom have as great an experience of the way in which our people in Canada live as any other group in this country, to think of how great a difference this will make in the lives of the individual citizens and children of this country.
This measure should be supported by everyone as a great social and humanitarian measure. The well-being of the individual is the supreme end of society, and the place to start is with the children. Many of us in this house have at one time or another talked about the great future that Canada will have. The place to start in making that future great is with the children of this country, with their nutrition, their health, their welfare and their education. Under this bill there will be paid each month to each parent a sum of money earmarked to meet the urgent needs of the children of our country.
This bill should also be supported as a great democratic .measure because it endeavours to create a greater equality of opportunity for all the children of Canada. It is a great Canadian measure because it treats all Canadians from end to end of the country absolutely alike. The leader of the opposition, in his speech as appears at page 5343 of the daily edition of Hansard, said among his objections to the measure, and I quote:
It denies the basic principles of social justice.
What reason did he give?' He said he objected to this measure because it treats all people alike. Well, I say that is one of the most extraordinary statements ever to be made in a democratic house by a democratic
Family Allowances

leader. He opposes this measure because it treats all people alike. I glory in its treating all people alike. The leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Parkdale and the Conservative press, before they even saw the measure, referred by innuendo or expressly to the fact that one part of Canada might be favoured by this measure more than another part. I deny that expressly. This measure treats all the citizens of Canada alike.

In Canada the discussion of this matter began a good many years back in 1929 when the predecessor of the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Blanchette), who spoke so well last night, Mr. J. E. Letellier de St. Just, introduced a resolution providing for family allowances. This was referred to the select standing committee on international and industrial relations. Last night the hon. member for Edmonton East referred to the Marsh report, the James report, and the report of the subcommittee of the James committee dealing with problems affecting women.
This subject is not new. It has been canvassed thoroughly here and in other parts of the world. When we step forward, as we are doing now, with a broader and more comprehensive and more generous measure than has been introduced in any part of the world as yet, we are showing the way to the rest of the world once again.
Hon. members may be interested in some figures relative to the number of children that may be involved. With the consent of the house I should like to put on Hansard a calculation of the cost of the family allowance resolution prepared by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics.
First this gives the estimated number of children in Canada on June 1, 1941. That figure is according to the census and particulars are given for children of different ages up to and including fifteen year's; the total is 3,409,911. That number has been extended by the procedure the bureau has to July 1, 1945, and for that date a total is shown of 3,535,934. While an increase is shown I may say to the house that the experience of other countries has been that the payment of family allowances does not result in a spectacular increase in the births in the country. It has some effect because conditions are straightened out in various ways, but there is no very spectacular result. The officials of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics inform me that it is not anticipated there will be a substantial change from the figure I give here, which is their estimate.

I had1 hoped at this time to be able to outline t-o the house my own/-and only my own-views as to how this would actually work out in administration. I see however that the time at my disposal has almost expired, and as hon. members have already been courteous and generous to me I believe I shall leave anything further I have to say until the bill is in committee. May I state briefly however that from government officials I have met I learn that it is their aim: first, to make the administration as simple as it can be made; second, to use all existing agencies of government that can be used; third, to arrive at, maintain and develop the closest possible cooperation with the provinces, and the agencies in the provinces; and fourth, to hope for and expect the development of all child welfare services and agencies which already exist and are doing such splendid work. But they could do even better work, because each of them finds that the fundamental obstacle in the way of continuous social betterment is the need for a greater income per child in each family. I can tell the house after a good deal of association with child welfare workers that it is clear that they believe this bill will change the whole character of their work. Instead1 of having to deal with conditions of extreme need and poverty, those welfare workers will be in a position to build so that the child, wherever it may be, under whatever conditions of life it may live, in whatever province it may be, and no matter who its father or mother may be, will have a better chance in its future life.
There has been some experience administratively in dealing with such large numbers. I am reminded that the dependents allowance board distributes 609,254 cheques per month. That is £C very large number. The provision for family allowances will lead to the distribution of something like 1,500,000 cheques per month. However, already a great deal of experience has been gained by treasury officials in administering arrangements of this kind. They believe that the three divisions into which administration will be divided, namely, registration, investigation and payment, can be adequately handled without any great or excessive cost. I saw in one publication that somebody estimated that the cost would be twenty per cent. The estimate arrived at based on the experience of similar measures in other countries and in other connections here would lead one to suppose that the cost will certainly not exceed two per cent, and will probably be less.

So, Mr. Speaker, we have here a measure which in no way interferes with the autonomy of the provinces, as was pointed out by the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent), and which does not purport to deal with education, as my hon. friend the member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion)_thqught. All that this purports to do^isTo"say what '" child is the kind of child that will receive the benefit, and this bill contemplates that it would not be the wish of anyone that a child who is working, or was a truant from school should receive the benefit. This bill treats the people of Canada from end to end alike,^ I support it and advocate its adoption and its enthusiastic support by the people of Canada as a great, progressive, constructive step in the building of the future society of our great country^

Mrs. DO RISE W. NIELSEN (North Battleford): Mr. Speaker, those of us who have been members of this parliament during these difficult years of the war emergency have had very many controversial issues come before us when it has not always been easy to see clearly the direction we should take, but it would appear to me with respect to this measure which is now before the house that any member who believes in the destiny and in the future of the younger generation of Canada can have no doubt whatever as to the advisability of giving it whole-hearted support. For my own self I feel very glad that I am a member of this House of Commons at this time and that even before the war is brought to its successful conclusion we have had an opportunity of seeing this legislation brought down to be put on the statute books of Canada.
I know that it is the duty of members of this house to look at any measure of national importance as objectively as possible, and yet I find that my own personal feelings do to some degree become mixed up in this. You see, I happen to be one of those unfortunate young women who belong to the generation in Canada who married and started to raise a young family during the most difficult days of the darkest period in the world's history. I know from first-hand experience of the struggles and the difficulties and all the heartaches of mothers who through those years sought to protect and bring up their children and to give them the best they could under such difficult conditions. Possibly there are those among the members of this house who suffered as I did; I do not know. It was a very terrible thing to lose a first son for lack of medical attention. It will always be a source of sorrow to me to know that one of my other children will suffer to the end of his days from physical disabilities which were caused through malnutrition in his early days. It was possibly because of my own sufferings that since I came into this house I have spent a great deal of my time speaking on the need for the introduction of social services to safeguard the life of our younger generation. Of course, the nazi menace reached a point where it overshadowed every other consideration, but to-day, when we find the beginning of the end within sight, it is a good thing that the government should at this time have turned its attention and concentrated upon a measure which will be the beginning of what we all hope to be a better and fuller life for the people of this country. Once on the statute book as a beginning, I sincerely hope that in time it may be 100-339J
broadened out and become part of a wider social security measure.
I think it is agreed by all of us that one of the great ends which this bill will achieve is the raising of the purchasing power of that section of our people who still need purchasing power so badly. It has long been recognized that the problem of production has been solved in the age in which we live. It has always been distribution that has been the snag. Lack of purchasing power, if we allow that to continue, will destroy the marvels that Canada is able to produce. The great productive forces of industry and agriculture which will be unleashed with the ending of this war will be futile to add to the progress of our nation unless we find it possible to increase and extend the abilities of wide sections of our people to consume that which they are able to produce. Certainly these family allowances will make a beginning in that direction.
Certain small sections of labour have registered some protest against this measure, and have even gone further and condemned it on the ground that it may be used as a means of keeping wages from rising after the war. I feel that that is a defeatist argument and that the great trade movement in this country will see to it that it is not so used. I believe that the great trade movement in this country will have the ability to defeat this argument and to prove the incorrectness of such a premise. I know that it will not stop the farm movement from working to secure the basic price guarantees that are needed for an upward adjustment of farm income in Canada.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was speaking in introducing this bill he mentioned that the cost of this measure was estimated to be in the neighbourhood of $250,000,000, and that of that roughly some $50,000,000 would be taken back through the income tax.
I am just wondering whether or not-I am not sure that I am correct-we shall obtain the greatest advantage from the expenditure of this money through grading the allowance to children according to age. Having a little family of my own, I realize that the cost of children does increase, generally speaking, as they grow older. But of course this family allowance is not a measure to cover completely the cost of upkeep of a child. I agree that it is a contribution towards the cost of upkeep. The Marsh report stated, I believe, that according to the rates of 1939, $14.50 monthly would be the minimum for the complete upkeep of a child. If we are to have a system of graded
Family Allowances

payments, it is going to be extremely difficult to administer. It will need a very large force of officials to check the authenticity of claims made, and so on. I am of the opinion that we could cut down the cost of administration and pay a greater part of that $200 million into the pockets of the people if we were to give a straight sum irrespective of the age of the child. Perhaps the Prime Minister in replying later will give arguments to prove that I am incorrect. I am quite open to persuasion on this matter, but it seems to me, from the little I know about administrative costs, that having the graded system would reduce the amount available for grants under this measure.
Another point of which I am not quite sure is whether it is wise to decrease the allowance to the larger family. I feel that it is unfair to the larger family. Perhaps food bought in larger quantities does not increase in cost in direct relation to the number of children, but certainly with regard to clothing, housing and .schooling the expenses increase with the size of the family. If we are to protect the health of the mothers of this nation; if the mother who has a large family is to maintain her health and strength, she needs assistance in her work. It has been said outside this chamber- I have noticed it in the press-that the gradation is for political reasons, that had we allowed family payments in the same amount to be applied in respect of any number of children it would have been said in some circles that this was a political sop to the province of Quebec. I wish to speak about this very frankly. I am an English-speaking Canadian, yet I would not regard any such measure as a sop to Quebec. I am aware that certain inequalities exist in that province, and I cannot believe that the future of Canada will be secure unless we keep the national unity we have and make it stronger, and we have to eradicate as far as possible inequalities among our people. To give a family allowance of equal amount per child to any size of family would have helped in some slight degree to remedy the inequalities which exist in Quebec. I think we should remember that those who sow the wind usually reap the whirlwind. Had the people of Germany not held legitimate grievances it would not have been possible for the nazis to prey upon them and exploit and inflame their grievances with such disastrous consequences. The people of Quebec have certain legitimate grievances. Their wage rates have always been lower than those of the majority of other provinces. Their living standards have been consequently lower, their disease rates have been higher; and but for these legitimate grievances we would not

to-day have certain groups trying to capitalize on those grievances with possibly disastrous results not only to Quebec but to the rest of Canada.
As the bill stands it militates against the French-Canadian people of Quebec. According to the census bulletin on households, occupations and earnings, No. 5, issued in 1941, I believe it is a fairly reliable estimate that while the province of Quebec has only about 24-8 per cent of the total number of families in Canada, it has 34-8 per cent of the families with five children, 43-5 per cent of the families with six or seven children, and 56-7 per cent of the families with eight or more children. There is no reason why any mother anywhere in Canada should not have adequate help and assistance, however many children she has.
This question of the size of the family is rather a delicate one to deal with in this house. A woman does not always have the right to decide how many children she shall have, yet the burden of the care and the constant work which attend the keeping of a large family is hers, and I am sorry, speaking personally, that the woman with the larger family will not receive the allowance which I feel she should have.
The Prime Minister, when he was speaking before, said he did not think that any very large section of the people would misuse this allowance. I agree with him. The twenty-fourth annual report of the Canadian Welfare Council supports the Prime Minister's statement. In this report, dated May 15, 1944, I find this statement:
In any event it seems fair that the success or failure of a children's allowance scheme will depend very largely on the proper development of an adequate administrative plan, and this is now being studied by the federal authorities. It will depend even more on the success of the arrangements which must be worked out to secure proper supervision and control over that small percentage of cases where the allowance would not otherwise be wisely handled.
This is the point I would1 like to emphasize.
The experience of the dependents' allowance board during the war years would seem to indicate that this percentage will not exceed more than one to three per cent of all cases.
That is an extremely low estimate. I still feel, as I said before when speaking on the bill setting up the Department of National Health and Welfare, that we should accompany these family allowances with a wide circulation of educational bulletins on all matters concerning the feeding and care and upbringing of children to give parents the knowledge which is necessary. If the allowance is not wisely spent, I believe that in the

Family Allowances
cases-the small percentage of cases-where it may not be wisely spent it will not be because of wilful misspending; it will be chiefly because of lack of knowledge as to how the money should be spent most advantageously in the interest of the childen.
I would quote again from the same report of the Canadian Welfare Council, where this is stated:
This points, in other words, to the conclusion *that we are not really faced with such a clear-cut alternative of cash allowances versus extended children's services, as the arguments presented on both sides of this much-debated question might appear to suggest. It is probable, almost to the point of certainty, that if we are to have cash allowances for children, we will also be obliged to extend and strengthen our children's services as well, in order to safeguard and control such a substantial national investment.
I feel that an organization such as the division of nutrition, headed by Doctor Pett, and certain other branches of the Department of Health and Welfare, would be only too glad to have the opportunity of presenting in bulletin form to the people of this country all the facts which would help the mothers to understand those factors of nutrition and so on which affect the health of their children.
There is one other thing which is a little surprising to me. I do not know whether I shall have support from any other hon. members on this particular question. I am wondering why, where the bill indicates to whom the allowance shall be paid, it mentions specifically first of all the father. I believe I am correct in understanding that the cheques' will be made payable to the father of the family. Of course, legally speaking, a married man is head of his household; I have no quarrel with that. But this allowance is not for general household expenditures. It is a special allowance which we hope will be used for the benefit of the children, and it is the women who are most elosely concerned with the welfare of the children. In a home where there is a real partnership the woman does usually have an allowance for housekeeping and for her own uses as well. But that is not always so. I feel of course that where a woman does have certain allowance for her own uses and for housekeeping expenses it is a good thing, and gives a married woman a feeling of independence which is very necessary, but unfortunately that does not exist in all homes. I wish it did. There are many homes where [DOT] that is not true. Women take an awful chance on this when they get married. So far as I know, there is no law which allows a woman to claim any part of her husband's wages as her share for the work she has to do in taking care of the family and the home.
In my own experience among rural people I have found that farm women suffer more than their city sisters do in this respect. It is a degrading thing for a woman to have to ask for every cent she wants for the expenditures in the home and for her own private needs, and yet that is precisely the case particularly in farming areas. I have found among many sections of the country, not only among foreign-born but among a good many Englishspeaking people also, that it is the man who, with his grain cheques or his hog cheques, pays the bills at the store, and the woman never actually has the handling of money. The independence of women is a very necessary thing if the women of this country are to go forward and attain that stature of fidl citizenship which they should have. I think that the great majority of the heads of households, the fathers, will pass over the cheques to their wives for the upkeep of the children. Well, if they do, why not pay it directly to the women, and so protect the women whose husbands will not automatically do it? It would be a good thing.
I would remind the Prime Minister of a very old saying. I have repeated it many times, and' no man has ever yet dared to dispute it with me. It is this: The rooster crows, but the hen it is that delivers the egg. It is all very well for the father or the husband to show off his beautiful children and their tricks, but it is the woman who has the daily care and responsibility as well as all the trouble that is connected with the upbringing of children. I would like to see the rights of women protected. I believe there is still great need for us to consider this question. After all, the place of the women in a country is a great indication of the advance of that particular society, and fhere is no real democracy without full equality between the sexes. But we are still a long way from that goal in [DOT]Canada. I would have been glad to see such a principle embodied in the bill, providing for payment of cheques directly to the mothers. I am not sure, but I believe that in section 6 it is provided that if a person is dissatisfied about this allowance that person will have the right to claim an adjustment. If a woman is going to be free under section 6 to claim the right to the allowance, if her husband does not give it to her, why not give it to her in the first place and so obviate additional administrative costs? I suggest that it would obviate a lot of such costs.

I am very glad indeed to hear the Prime Minister say that; it relieves my mind considerably. But I wonder what will determine the matter in some homes. Is it going to be a question of individually finding out whether the husband or the wife should have the cheque? I fail to see what will be used as a guide in the matter. I still adhere to my belief that it would cost less in the long run in administration to pay the cheque directly to the woman.
However, I am in full agreement with the bill. As we come to the separate sections there may be a few other remarks I would like to make. I am not just sure about section 6, in which it is stated that if any person is dissatisfied with the way the money is being spent, that person can appeal. I do not know whether that will affect neighbours or gossips or people who for some slight reason or other may have some feeling against a woman. We have to be very careful of the rights of people to appeal. At any rate, I shall be able to deal with these points when the sections come up before us. Generally speaking, I am proud to be able to give support to a bill of this kind, and I only hope we shall see other measures which will continue the social security of our people so that we may go forward in the same direction as this proposal.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
maintopic: CALCULATION OF COST OF FAMILY ALLOWANCE RESOLUTION
speechtext:
Following the hon. member who has just spoken, I am sure that I express the feelings of every member of the house-and the same will apply to the observations last fevening of the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mrs. Casselman) -when I say we recognize that no group of members in this house have more right to speak in support of this measure than the hon. member who has just taken her seat and her lady colleague who sits on this side of the house. It may be that in considering this measure the house is not only providing for the future citizens of the country but is also thereby, by implication, paying a long overdue tribute to the mothers of Canada. I am reminded, in taking part in this debate, of the words of Pitt, who, speaking in the House of Commons on an amendment to the Poor Laws, said on February 12, 1796:
Let us make relief in cases where there are a number of children a matter of right and an honour, instead of a ground for opprobrium and contempt. This will make a large family a blessing and not a curse, and this will draw a proper line of distinction between those who are able to provide for themselves by their
[Mr. Mackenzie King.l
labour, and those who, after having enriched their country with a number of children, have a claim upon its assistance for their support.
I wonder if I would be regarded as unfair if I suggested to the hon. member for Park-dale (Mr. Bruce), who spoke last night, that he should take to heart these words of Pitt and realize that in referring to the children of our country there is no occasion for irony or for anything approaching what I regard as his contemptuous observations of last evening.
This particular measure now before the house is a part of the government's programme of social security. It is not the first plank in that platform. Perhaps the first real measure came with the introduction of unemployment insurance in 1940, under which scheme now two millions of our citizens will share in a fund contributed to by workers, by employers and by the government and amounting to over $205 million. In that unemployment insurance scheme, based upon the experience that other countries have had, an attempt is being made to improve where others failed, and it is now being followed by this measure, which I think Mr. Beveridge, Mr. Marsh and Alvin Hanson have said is the first necessary condition in any real social security programme.
I must say that I was not a little disturbed when I found the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon), speaking for a great historic party in this country, failing to fall in step not only with progressive thought throughout Canada but with progressive thought throughout the world. Recently at the twenty-sixth meeting of the international labour conference forty-two nations of the world, representing employers, workers and governments, met, and among the things that they all recommended for adoption in their own countries was a system of family allowances on the basis of the Australian model, which we are following in large measure in this house. In 1938 I find that at the pan-Ameriean conference of twenty-one American republics a recommendation was made that family allowances be set up in eveiy one of those twenty-one republics.
This is not a matter of bribe; this is a matter which in the growing process of history has come to be recognized by all men as part of the very necessary assignment of the state in the duty it owes to its citizens, and particularly to those within the low income brackets. We have given expression in the Atlantic charter to such declarations as freedom from want. What steps are we to take in order to give effect to freedom from want unless we give support to this kind of measure, unless we hurriedly recognize that we cannot wait until we set up a complete system of social

Family Allowances
services, which in answer to the leader of the opposition I tried to suggest yesterday would take many years to achieve on the basis of the evidence given by Doctor Davidson before [DOT]the social security committee of this parliament.
No; freedom from want will follow statesmen and governments throughout the ensuing decades in a manner which perhaps many of us at this stage are unwilling to recognize; and while we have taken a great step in this measure I venture to suggest that in ten years from now this measure, commendable as it is now, will be looked upon as something that is only part of many of the things which must be done to justify our commitment to the general expression throughout the world that there .must be freedom from want. Mr. Beveridge, Alvin Hanson, Mr. Keynes, all the great sociologists and economists of our day have recognized that a system of social security without a system of family allowances is not a system of social security at all. Mr. Keynes has gone on to say that a high level of employment is not possible in Britain unless they have along with it a kind of scheme of family allowances. This latter plan differs from that of Sir William Beveridge.
Thirty-four countries-in Europe; Australia, Japan, New Zealand, some of them since the end and one before the beginning of the last war-have adopted this measure in principle; yet it was left to the leader of the opposition and to his group to be the only voice in Canada opposing the principle of this measure. This is an attack on poverty, and poverty we have-every country has. Poverty exists throughout the world. We have poverty which we hope to mitigate by covering children's maintenance and subsistence, such things as food, clothing, light and fuel. And as one who has had something to do with the Department of Labour, I say that we will find under a system of family allowance one of the ready means of taking care of the problem of over-insurance about which I shall have more to say in a few moments.
As has been said, we are merely extending the principle which we have recognized in old age pensions, in the income tax exemptions, in mothers' allowances and dependents' allowances. It is the same kind of principle, only we are extending it to groups who for one reason or another cannot qualify within the income tax-paying brackets. The fact is that every addition to a family is an additional economic handicap. No one who comes from a large famity, no one who has felt what it is to want, no one who has aspired to positions of greatness in public life or in industry and who has come from a small home with a large
family, can fail to recognize that a large family is an economic handicap; and in providing this additional opportunity by way of perhaps better food, perhaps assisting in better housing, certainly I hope in better education, we are taking a step which in the days to come those of us who are members of this parliament shall not regret. For the fact is that the future citizens of our country have a value to society just as much as our forests, just as much as the development of our national resources upon which the richness of our economy depends. Yet we spend less time and less interest on our children. We have been charged with being emotional, with being excitable, because we lay emphasis on the fact that there are some things in life more important than purely economic and material things.
There is no relation between the size of a man's family and the remuneration which he receives, as I hope to show in dealing with the labour aspect of this problem; there is no possible way of bringing that differential into line. No, Mr. Speaker; family allowances cannot help but be regarded as the way of first guaranteeing a continuing assurance of income regardless of what happens to the father. There is no man or woman in this house who has not seen what the spectre of death can bring to homes where there are no means of carrying on in the absence of the father. Family allowances are a subvention, not a provision for family standards, but an aid to family standards. They will assist the worker who is exposed to a variety of hazards beyond his capacity to control. As I said, we spend money on land, forests and1 factories and the other material assets of this nation. But in the past I think we have not placed sufficient emphasis upon human values. As the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Claxton) said, in the days that lie ahead, when we shall have to dovetail private initiative into a system of public investment to keep men at gainful work rather than in receipt of the dole, we shall find that this fund of $200,000,000 will serve as a very effective part of that public investment programme. It will serve to provide additional purchasing power as well as to guarantee against insecurity and the like.
There are those who suggest, and the leader of the opposition was one, that instead of direct allowances we should have allowances in kind; that instead of giving money to the father or the mother for the children we should provide sendees in the form of better housing, more milk for the children, hot meals for the children at school and the like. Well,
Family Allowances

I ask him to ask the person who advised him in the remarks he made in this house what she would have to say about a report made in Norway in 1938, where after a careful study some Norwegians, assisted by a group of Englishmen and a group of experts from other countries, recommended that in respect of housing and medical attention collective effort was of special value, but when it came to the everyday things of life, there was, upon examination, only one system which would serve those things and that was a system of family allowances, not based upon the practice of France but based upon the practice embodied in this bill, a direct contributory scheme, not from employers and workers directly, but a scheme directly contributed to by the state, allowing for full control by the government with no intervention by industry or other groups.
I was not a little surprised that the leader of the opposition should have made the remarks he did about this bill, especially in the light of the study made with regard to family allowances by a gentleman, a former distinguished law partner of mine and a man for whom I have the highest personal regard and who was chairman of the national war labour board. He recommended a system of family allowances.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
maintopic: CALCULATION OF COST OF FAMILY ALLOWANCE RESOLUTION
speechtext:
Yes. In one breath "yes" and in another breath, " no." Mr. Justice McTague, now Mr. McTague, said in His report:
We are aware that family allowances usually find their place in a general programme of social security rather as a part of a wage control policy, but substandard wages are indefensible at all times and if control of wages below 50 cents is not removed the solution is a system of family allowance.
That is undoubtedly what the hon. gentleman had in mind. For the first time in the history of this country someone recommended the very thing the leader of the opposition opposed. In that statement Mr. Justice McTague was recommending family allowances as a substitute for low wages, the very thing which we in this bill are trying to avoid and the very thing which the leader of the opposition said we must try to avoid. Yet a month later the same gentleman, now the organizer of the Conservative party, now a candidate for office in the next parliament of Canada, said:
There is no use glibly talking about family allowances being a substitute for wages. No one suggests it is. It represents a measure of social security to people whose status really requires it.

I believe that statement of Mr. McTague was correct. But I put that statement alongside the statement made by Mr. Bracken on June 25 and the statement made yesterday in this house by the leader of the opposition. If the Prime Minister or the government of this country is guilty of introducing this measure for one provocation or for one purpose or another, then what is to be said of the chief of the Conservative party organization who gave expression to the very same view? Obviously we are motivated1 in trying to bring about a system of family allowances because we know that under a capitalistic or socialistic form of society there are defects in the wage system which I do not think can adequately be met. There seem to be three main defects.
First, the amount of money required to maintain a family depends upon the number of people going to make up that family. Existing wage payments are made for the work performed and not according to the size of a man's family. Is there any other way of dealing with that anomaly? Second, the expenses of keeping up a family vary with the ages of the children. A father needs the most help when his income is generally low, at a time when his family is at the top level in so far as numbers are concerned. Generally the father is making less when the needs of his family are greatest. Third, in looking after individuals the state provides for them according to their real rather than their imaginary needs. The effect of this is that often it is more advantageous for a man with a number of children to be unemployed. That was the experience in Great Britain in connection with the administration of unemployment insurance, and about that Sir William Beveridge had this to say:
The only way to keep the difference between income during employment and during unemployment as large as possible, and at the same time to keep benefits adequate during unemployment and disability, is to give allowances for children in time of earning and non-earning alike.
That great precursor of reform, Mrs. Sidney Webb-I invite those sections of labour in this country who may still have doubts to bear in mind what she said-had this to say in her minority report to the British government in 1919:
. . ._ the community must face the necessity of seeing that adequate provision is made for children, not by statistical averages, but case by case. The average family is, of course, merely a convenient figment of the statistician's and does not exist in fact. If provision is made in one way er another for three children, this is very far from securing enough food and adequate conditions of nurture for those households in which there are, for years in succession, four, five, or more children dependent. The nation

Family Allowances
cannot be satisfied any more than children can with a family or household average of rations for the rising generation. Each individual baby has got to be adequately and satisfactorily provided for.
That was in 1919. That is the observation of a woman who recognized the defects in the wage system under both the capitalistic and socialistic form of society. She was away ahead of her time, but she recommended the sort of thing we are dealing with now.
I do not think anyone has met this problem more accurately than the present Prime Minister of Australia. In 1929, as a member of the royal commission investigating the problem, he was faced with the apathy, and in many quarters with the criticism of his own party because of a dissenting report he had made recommending family allowances as opposed to the majority report. In his statement Mr. Curtin goes on to say that there is no real connection between the system of family allowances we are envisaging in this bill, and what they now have in Australia, and the general level of wages. This is particularly so because in each country there is a great section of the population who are in a non-wage earning group. Forty per cent of the people in this country are in the non-wage earning group. Even assuming the validity of the argument put forward yesterday by the leader of the opposition, even assuming that it has merit, what about the forty per cent of our people, our farm people, who are not wage earners as such and who because of their low income status are undoubtedly wanting in food and other necessities which in this day and age cannot be denied?
There is one aspect of the problem I should like to deal with. I am glad to hear from the lips of the hon. member who has spoken, and from the leader of the C.C.F., that they support this measure. It will be remembered that some sections of labour did oppose this bill. When the matter was first introduced some sections of labour did express apprehension and concern. They said it might be used as a depressive for wages. What are the facts? I think one should speak plainly in this matter because of the tremendous benefits the wage earning class of this country will derive.
In Great Britain there was some apprehension about this matter. The trade union movement in that country was concerned about the proposal to adopt a system of family allowances. It was felt that as in France the employers would take advantage of this kind of assistance and pay lower wages to their workers. One group after another expressed opposition. But in 1927 the
British trade unions stopped their opposition. A majority report of the joint committee of the trade union council and the British labour party executives stated that they had arrived at the conclusion that the most valuable step that could be taken to further the welfare of the nation's children was the institution of a scheme of family allowances. Later the trade union congress as well as the Labour party gave expression to the same kind of view. I call the attention of the house to the words of a great British trade union leader, Mr. James Griffiths, M.P., who said:
I would feel more resolved and more determined facing the employers, if I knew the children of the men for whom I was negotiating were outside of the power of the owners to starve if conflict came.
I use those words, and I ask labour throughout the country to remember them. No one in his good senses to-day will doubt the right of labour to organize. The fact is that to-day in this country we have a trade union membership of 700,000, as compared with about 300,000 at the beginning of the war. In my opinion that is a good thing, not only for the workers but for Canada. As long as we have an informed trade union movement, as we have in this country, one which I repeat is good for Canada and good for the workers themselves, there need be no fear on the part of labour that the system of family allowances will be used as a weapon by irresponsible employers. I think of the words of Mr. Griffiths, when he said he would feel safer if he knew his children and the children of his colleagues in the plant were to be provided with the necessities of life during a stoppage of work, than he would under the old system where the opportunity of dealing with employers was always rendered one-sided because of the fact that workers themselves did not have the wherewithal to provide the necessities for their dependents during the out-of-work period.
This is the attitude of labour. Labour throughout the whole of the united nations at the recent international labour conference clearly showed where labour, generally speaking, stands on the subject. I am sure all ranks of labour in this country, when they really consider this matter in the light in which we are discussing it to-day, will see that it cannot be used as a depressant, and that it is not to be used as a depressant; and as long as they have strong trade union organizations-which this government has encouraged-they need not be afraid.
There is the view also of the British Labour party, and the trade union congress in 1930, signed not only by a majority of the committee but by a majority of the trade unionists

Family Allowances

on it. They were firm in their views with respect to a system of family allowances, and the joint committee said:
Indeed, we believe that daring industrial conflicts the unions will be very considerably helped by the existence of such a scheme since the workers' children will be removed from the firing line and a great factor of weakness will then be removed.
May I say that I was glad to hear the leader of the C.C.F. support the view of the Prime Minister to the effect that this measure was not a means of depressing wages, but rather a means of supplementing something which wages cannot take into account-the number of children a married man may or may not have. But under no circumstances should we encourage in any way, or should this measure in any way be regarded as an encouragement to industry, large or small, to take advantage of the situation unwittingly to reduce wages, or to take into account wage costs in relation to this matter.
We have reached the stage when we have to have a different conception of the place of industry in society, a conception of industry where the partner is not only the man whose interest is that of investments, but as well the man who gives his services as manager and the man who gives his energy as a worker. These two last named partners have their rights in industry just as much as have the investors. Industry will have to come to recognize that. Just as it is entitled to depreciation on its machinery, it should provide through reserve funds and the like for depreciation of the human beings engaged in industry, and who make to industry an immeasurable contribution. That contribution is much greater than the contribution rendered by the tools or the equipment, buildings and the like in modern industry.
This is a forward measure. We are in the throes of transition. We do know that great changes are taking place. As we go along, measures which now are considered by some to be excessive, in the course of time will be regarded as only part and parcel of a world which is gradually developing, and which now is not wholly apparent to us.
John Curtin, the Prime Minister of Australia, was charged by individuals in his own country, when he wrote his minority report of 1929, with giving encouragement to a system by which wages would certainly be depressed. He said throughout Australia, as every labour man in this country who has studied the matter now knows, that as long as labour is strong, as long as the government recognizes the privileges as well as the obligations of labour, and as long as labour is able to

organize for its own use as well as for the community, these dangers may not be regarded as at all serious. He went further than that, and used in support of Bill 116 in the House of Representatives of Australia in 1941, words which I shall use as my closing remarks to-day. I believe these words represent what is in the mind of each member who gives his support to this measure. They are:
With this bill we are, for the first time in the history of this country-writing into the statute book our realization of the national significance of family life. That is not a mere platitude- that means something. There never has been any doubt of the value of the services, infinite in variety and extent, which the family renders to the nation. Primarily, it is a source of national continuance: it has supplied the human material indispensable for the production of the means of subsistence; it provides for the replacement of the old and the dead, and is a sole guarantee for the redemption, in the future, of those obligations which previous and present generations have found it desirable to incur in order to enjoy the fullest obtainable measures of security, comfort and civilization . . . therefore, every contribution we can make to the improvement of the health and welfare of the children now growing up is a definite contribution to the stability of the national structure in the years to come.

speakeroldname: Mr. S. H. KNOWLES (Winnipeg North Centre):
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: CALCULATION OF COST OF FAMILY ALLOWANCE RESOLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as has already been pointed out by the leader of this group, we of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation welcome wholeheartedly the introduction of this measure. We feel, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) suggested yesterday, that its introduction is a tribute to the work that a great many social pioneers have done in this and other countries down through the years, in endeavouring to propagate some of the principles now being enunciated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I refer in particular to his statement that we are members one of another, and that as a community we owe a joint responsibility to our entire citizenry.
I am sure the Prime Minister would be the first to agree with the statement made yesterday by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that, in part at least, this legislation is a tribute to the work carried on for so many years by the statesman I had the honour to succeed as member for the constituency of Winnipeg North Centre, the late J. S. Woodsworth. It must be remembered that it is not very long ago that we of the C.C.F. were criticized for advocating policies in the name of social security which, it was charged, would bring about the degeneration of our Canadian people. We were of the opinion then, as we are to-day, that human beings- and we were speaking specially of Canadians *-are made of good stuff, and the better the

Family Allowances
opportunities for life surrounding our people, the more of initiative and character and resourcefulness will be displayed by them. Accordingly, we support wholeheartedly every move that aims at improving the economic security of all our people.
When the Prime Minister says as he did yesterday that if we mean business when we talk about freedom from want and freedom from fear and about implementing the terms of the Atlantic charter we must do something about it, we must take some concrete steps, I say that in this instance he was reflecting the views of the Canadian people. I am satisfied that there is in this country at the present time a determination, expressed by the phrase that is used so often, that this time not only must we win the war but we must win the peace. Accordingly, I hope that this measure is only one step looking in the direction of a wider and all-inclusive programme of social security that we shall have in this country not very long hence.
The leader of this group pointed out that our major comment in connection with this bill is not one of criticism but is one of tribute to it when we say that we wish it were part of a still larger programme of social security. Members of parliament, it seems to me, should be particularly conscious of this necessity because of the many cases of individual need with which we are called upon to deal. We find time and again that after we have passed this or that desirable piece of social legislation, although it may take care of certain cases, yet there are always coming to us other cases that are not taken care of by these piecemeal steps. For example, parliament provided a special allowance last session for widows of veterans of the last war, veterans who at their death were in receipt of a fifty per cent pension or less. That was a token or gesture in the right direction, but the provision covered only widows of such veterans as had served in an actual theatre of war. England was not so regarded in the last war. The consequence is that we as members of parliament run into many cases of widows whose husbands were volunteers and served during the greater part or all of the last war but did not get to France, and their widows by reason of that technicality are not given the allowance. The widow herself stands in just as great need of it as her sister whose husband did get to France, but there is no provision to cover her need. We continually run up against technicalities like that which underline the necessity of our getting out of this stage of piecemeal social legislation as quickly as we can in favour of an all-inclusive plan.
100-340i
So it is with unemployment insurance, a commendable measure which was brought down by this government. As I pointed out the other night, we run into many cases of employees who have made their payments into the unemployment insurance fund and then have to lay off work because of illness. They find that they are not covered by the premiums which they have paid into the unemployment insurance fund; yet they are unemployed and their income stops. They are assailed by an economic condition which is not covered by the act, and real hardship results. That situation also underlines the necessity of an allinclusive programme of social legislation.
I wish to make it clear, Mr. Speaker, that in making these suggestions I am not talking just to find fault with this measure. Rather I am sincerely and earnestly urging that now that we have gone this far in accepting the principles underlying this measure, we by no means stop there.
I should like to deal with the argument referred to by the last speaker and by some others who have participated in this debate, namely, the fear that family allowances might be used to depress wages. It is perfectly true that certain sections of organized labour have had that fear; some of them still have it. That fear is based on some sad experiences which organized labour has had with certain government departments and boards, and also in its dealings with vested interests. It is also based on the fact that so far as our peacetime arrangements are concerned, the control of labour legislation, working conditions, collective bargaining and minimum wages, is still in the hands of the provinces, whereas this provision for family allowances is being made by the dominion government. It would be far better if both were under the same jurisdiction, and some of this fear would be allayed if we were a little more certain that in the not far distant future control of these matters affecting working conditions, collective bargaining and wages would be in the hands of this same branch of government which is making provision for family allowances. I urge the securing of those necessary powers for the dominion government. In doing so, I want to point out that, as I see it, it is by no means a case of interfering with the rights of the people of our various provinces. It would be an interference, long overdue, with the power of vested interests at the present time to play upon the slogan of provincial rights in order to keep wages and working conditions depressed in some provinces as compared with others, to the detriment of all the people of Canada. I hope that leadership might be given to the people of all our provinces, as
Family Allowances

Canadians, to the effect that it is in. their own interest to have matters of this kind made the concern of the federal government. There is no reason at all why we cannot write a bill of rights that would give an absolute and inviolable guarantee to our provinces over certain matters of a cultural nature which are sacred to them. But so far as matters of this kind are concerned, which bear upon the economic status and the life and well-being of our people as Canadians, it seems to me that we should move, without further delay, in the direction that I have already indicated. I suggest that if we were moving more clearly in that direction it would allay some of the fear about family allowances depressing wage standards. I recognize the steps that have been taken in this direction so far as war-time conditions are concerned. I hope that there may be no retreat from that position.
But even so, Mr. Speaker, I am not worried about the introduction of family allowances depressing wages or the working conditions of our people. For one reason, public opinion is too strong on this point. The people of Canada have done a great deal of thinking about social and economic matters in the last ten years and particularly during the years of the war. It is also true then when people have their standards raised a bit, that is the very time when you cannot turn around and push them down. It is when people are most deeply depressed that they can be most easily taken advantage of. When people are on the way up, when they are feeling their position and having their importance in society recognized, not just 'by talk but by something real like this measure, they become stronger and less subject to abuse at the hands of vested interests.
I should like to quote a sentence or two from an opinion expressed by the joint committee of the labour party and trades union congress in England in 1930 on this matter, when they said:
During industrial conflicts the unions will be very considerably helped by the existence of such a scheme-
The reference was to children's allowances. -since the workers' children will be removed from the firing line and a great factor of weakness thus removed.
I submit that at the present time the worker's bargaining position is weakened by . the fact that his wife and children are dependent upon him to the very limit. But if there were a certain amount of independence for his wife and children-I use the words "certain amount" advisedly, because this is not very much in the way of "independence"-it removes his wife and family from the firing

line and strengthens the position of the employee in bargaining with his employer.
I submit, for example, that the introduction of unemployment insurance has not weakened, but rather it has strengthened the position of labour and of the trade union movement. The fact is that labour's position and the strength of the trade union movement are much greater in Canada to-day than they ever were. Therefore I am confident that this move will not result in a depression of wages or working conditions. For one thing, as I said at the outset of this section of my remarks, public opinion in Canada and the trade union movement simply would not stand for it.
Another argument which is sometimes used against family allowances in cash is that instead of these allowances we should have improved welfare services. The argument implies that, rather than run the risk of giving cash to people who might not spend it as wisely as they should-a false and unworthy argument-it would be better for the community to organize social and welfare services which will see to it that the proper care is provided for the children. In my view it is not a case of one or the other; we should have both. By this I mean that there are some things which can best be done on a community basis. There are some things which will serve our children best if we have them organized as welfare services. But even after you have done that, we in this country place a very high premium upon family life, upon the independence of the family, upon the relationship between parents and children. Consequently I think it is most desirable that an effort should be made to put into the hands of parents cash to equalize as far as possible the position with respect to their children, and the control of that extra money should be in the hands of the parents themselves. So that I say it is not a case of one or the other of these two things; we should have both; and I trust that in the years which lie ahead we shall have an increase in the amount of the family allowances, and also that as we go along we shall improve the services by which we minister to the needs and the welfare and the health of our children.
Another argument which is sometimes used is that instead of providing family allowances the government should allow wages to go up. That would be a trap for labour to fall into if it did not have its eyes open. As a matter of fact, in the days before we had a wagefreezing policy, in other words when theoretically it was possible for wages to rise, they did not do so. We had thousands of families in this country living under depressed conditions and children suffering from malnutrition.

Family Allowances
It is a case not of one or the other but of both. Our economy should be such that the wage income of our workers can increase, and at the same time we need the implementing of this measure so that there may be an equalization of the physical opportunities for children in various families.	_
There are a few comments which I should like to make about the bill and which I trust the Prime Minister will accept as constructive even though they may seem to. be critical.
I am not offering these suggestions out of a desire to find something wrong, but rather in the hope that my suggestions may be given consideration. I suppose that the course which will be followed with respect to this measure ' ' is this. This bill will be passed substantially in its present form; there may be some minor amendments, although one cannot be too sure of that. It is not to come into effect until July 1, 1945. In the meantime there will be another session of parliament, either of this parliament or the next one. My notion is that in the meantime further study will have been given to some of these matters such as I am going to speak about, and we shall probably have an amending act next year so as to take care of some of these matters before the measure comes into effect.
The first suggestion I would make is that payment of family allowances should be divorced from our income tax structure. As it now stands, it is too complicated and will create some rather odd, if not bad, psychological situations. On the one hand, you have people being given the family allowances -all families where there are children of the prescribed ages. On the other hand, in many cases the family allowance is to be taken back by an offset against income tax exemptions. I submit that that is going to puzzle a good many people and may even have the effect of making them feel that it is not such a good measure after all, and I for one do not want to see a social security measure of this kind come into disrepute in any way. The bill states in section 7, and the government has given publicity to the fact, that no allowances under this measure are to be subject to taxation; but in section 8 of the bill it is provided that there can be the taking back of family allowances as an offset against exemptions or benefits provided under the Income War Tax Act. What you have there is really just a confusion of terms. The allowance is not subject to taxation, and yet roughly speaking, for those with between $1,200 and $1,800 a year, depending upon the number of children in the family and then-ages, a portion of that family allowance will be taken back. The bill says it is not taxed.
Technically that is correct, but actually a portion of it is taken back; in other words it is taxed. For those with over $1,800, or in some cases a little higher, depending again upon the number of children they have, they receive it and the whole of it is taken back. Technically it is not taxed, and yet it is definitely taken away from them, which amounts to the same thing. My fear about that is that people may develop a dislike for it, and I am concerned that we should avoid anything of that kind about a piece of social security legislation.
